content.thinking:
I need to write the entire piece carefully in one pass without testing along the way, so I'm planning the design upfront: a realistically-sized koala clinging to a eucalyptus branch mounted on a stand base, working out proportions and pose before committing to the full build.

I'll settle on a simpler pose: the koala's bottom rests on a short horizontal stub branch angled behind the trunk, with its torso leaning upright against the trunk, arms wrapping around at chest height, and hind legs splayed with feet gripping the trunk lower down.

Now mapping out the floor and dimensions: a wooden plinth box at y=0.03, trunk rising from y=0.06 to 1.3, koala seated with its hips around y=0.40-0.47 so its head lands near y=0.95-1.0, giving a total model height around 1.4m. I'm setting up the skeleton with hips at the root, then a spine chain running up through chest and neck to the head, keeping the torso nearly upright with a slight forward lean.

I'm working out the arm placement so the koala's limbs wrap around the trunk, with shoulders near y=0.80 and hands curling toward the back of the trunk to meet behind it.

But the head's radius overlaps the trunk, so I'm adjusting the trunk's position further out and tilting the head to the side like a real koala pressing its face against the tree.

Actually maybe I should rethink the whole pose: have the trunk positioned behind the koala as a diagonal branch fork, with the koala's back leaning into the crotch of the Y-branch, and arms reaching up to grip a branch in front instead of wrapping the same trunk the head presses against.

Still placing the seat branch so the koala straddles it at the thighs, then working out a hold branch curving up from the trunk toward the hands so the arms can wrap around it naturally.

I realize the branch geometry as planned would pass straight through the torso, which is wrong—I need to reposition the branch so it stays in front of the chest rather than intersecting it, adjusting the trunk-to-branch coordinates accordingly.

Trying another approach: maybe the koala simply hugs a vertical trunk positioned slightly forward, with the torso leaning into it and the head staying centered above, so I avoid needing a separate crossing branch altogether.

I'm adding a seat branch running from the trunk backward under the koala's bottom, then positioning the hind legs with hips and feet wrapping around the trunk, adjusting their height so they don't collide with the seat branch.

Checking arm segment distance between shoulder and hand gives about 0.275, close to the combined segment lengths of 0.29, so a slight outward bend works. I'm settling on using absolute world coordinates throughout, with +X as the left side, and setting hint directions outward for elbow bends.

For the paws, I'm placing the hand tip near the trunk surface and having 3-4 digit chains curl around toward the back, giving the koala hands their characteristic grip with a mix of fingers and opposable thumbs.

I'm working out how koala paws actually grip: two opposable thumbs wrapping toward the front of the trunk and three fingers wrapping toward the back, each digit offset slightly along the trunk's y-axis so they read as separate claws around the branch.

Now I'm figuring out how the digit chains attach to the arm skeleton — each finger/thumb chain needs to parent to the wrist joint at the tip of the arm's shoulder-elbow-wrist chain, so the hand digits inherit the correct position and orientation from wherever the arm ends.

I'll plan a helper function for digits so I can generate fingers and thumbs consistently, using simple point chains with appropriate joint counts. Keeping total joint count well under budget: roughly 20 for hands and 20 for feet across both sides.

For the feet, I'm handling the koala's five toes with the fused 2nd/3rd pair, treating it as three regular toes plus an opposable big toe, each with two joints, reusing the same digit helper as the hands but offset at the trunk position. I want to parameterize toe and finger angles so the same wrapping logic works for both hands and feet with different base coordinates.

Still working out digit geometry...

For the palm itself I'll use a flat dark grey box near the wrist to mimic koala paw pads, then move to the trunk, which I want to texture with smooth eucalyptus bark coloring along its vertical sweep.

For the pixel-art feel, I'm figuring out cell sizes relative to the koala's scale so the painted texture reads as blocky squares rather than smooth gradients, aiming for roughly 2mm texels across a ~3m² painted surface while keeping geometry low-sided and boxy to match that chunky aesthetic.

I'm settling on an 8-sided flat-shaded body sweep for the faceted voxel look, pairing it with cell-painted textures for the eyes, nose, inner ears, and leaves, and picking out a snapped gray fur ramp and cream belly palette to keep the colors within the limited pixel-art range.

Now I'm rounding out the full palette: black nose with a highlight, fluffy white inner ears, eucalyptus bark in tan-brown streaks, lanceolate blue-green leaf cards with dark veins, small brown gumnuts, and a wooden plank base with moss patches and a plinth stand.

I'm also planning the joint hierarchy for the rig, deciding to set a single root joint (like "stand" or "hips") near the base, with everything else parented up from there since only one root bone is allowed.

I'm now figuring out the spine chain, sketching a catmull-rom path through points like hips, mid-spine, chest, and neck, and debating how many spans and joint names to use so the tip connects cleanly to the neck chain.

Then I'm chaining the neck up to a head joint with a jaw child, making sure the hips joint parents correctly off the root "stand" joint, and starting to lay out the leg chains with hip, knee, ankle naming conventions.

For the legs I'm parenting them to the first spine joint and mirroring hip positions by side, then building arm chains off the chest spine joint with shoulder, elbow, wrist names. For the koala's ears, I'm planning flattened sphere shapes parented to the head, oriented outward with some added fluff detail cards for texture.

Placing the head using cell-paint shading with flat faceting for a faceted look, positioning it at world coordinates near the top of the body, and working out a short neck chain connecting the chest to the head joint.

Planning a single-joint neck chain and figuring out how the body loft sweep should span from spine through neck to cover that transition smoothly without gaps.

Using a bone list combining spine and neck for the loft should work since the spine chain's endpoint matches the neck's start. I'm now thinking through the torso loft stations — setting width and height for a pot-bellied, nearly neckless koala shape, with the sweep's radial axes aligned along the back and side directions.

I realize the end caps add extra height beyond the path endpoint, so my bottom station was sitting too low. I'm bumping the first station up to y=0.56 and reworking the sequence of stations upward from there to keep the seat bottom around 0.41.

Now I'm adding more stations toward the shoulders and head, then figuring out the hips and spine joint positions—placing the pelvis around (0,0.52,-0.07) and building a spine chain of points up through the torso, plus a short neck chain connecting to the head.

With the skeleton sorted, I'm designing the fur coloring: a cell-based paint that countershades the koala, blending gray on the back with cream on the chest and belly, using noise and normal direction to vary the gray tone, and adding pale rump patches with speckled spots plus lighter fur along the ear edges.

Adding paw and nose colors...

Now I'm shaping the head geometry — a scaled sphere positioned near the top with a lighter muzzle sphere for the snout, setting up where the large black koala nose will sit.

For the nose I'm going blocky and pixelated: a small textured box rather than a smooth shape, positioned on top of the muzzle with a tiny pixel-art texture (highlights and nostril dots) mapped to its faces, keeping with a chunky pixel-style aesthetic I'll also apply to the eyes.

Calculating eye position...

Now I'm sizing the jaw geometry, placing a small lower jaw box under the muzzle for the koala's tiny mouth, plus a jaw joint pivot to connect upper and lower jaw parts.

For the fluffy cheeks and ears, I'm scattering small fur tuft cards across the head surface using a pixelated tuft texture, varying their size and lean angle, and tinting them with the coat color paint to build up a fuzzy silhouette.

For the ears, I'm shaping them as large rounded koala ears with flattened discs positioned high on the head, tilting them to face outward and forward with white tufted detailing.

Working out ear sphere scale and inner-circle offset along the facing normal, then adding scattered white tuft cards around the ear edge for texture. Moving on to arm and leg sweeps with cel-shaded paint and tapering radius.

Now I'm working out the leg geometry — computing hip and knee positions using triangle math so the thigh and shin lengths connect properly with the knee bulging slightly forward for a natural bend.

I should nudge the knee outward using the pole hint so it doesn't sit inside the belly — using the plane formed by hip, target, and hint, I'm offsetting the knee perpendicular to the hip-target line, pushing it mostly in x with a bit of y, landing roughly around (0.1, 0.5, 0.13) plus that offset.

Now checking the hands and head placement against the trunk — the chest front surface leaves about a 0.09 gap from the trunk at the hand's height, which seems fine since the arms rest along the trunk sides, but I need to verify whether the head/cheek region clears the trunk near the top given the nose offset.

The trunk forks around y=0.93 into two diverging branches, and I'm checking whether this fork clips the nose — it's close, so shifting the trunk's z-position slightly outward should give enough clearance for the arm and hand placement too.

I'm nudging the fork branches to angle back slightly in z so they clear the nose, and checking the ear placement doesn't collide with the branches either—everything's sitting close but just barely separated.

Now I'm adding more eucalyptus foliage details: leaf clusters on the branch stub, plus additional branches extending sideways from the lower trunk with hanging leaf clusters, and defining the curve path for the left fork branch.

Checking that the branch doesn't collide with the hands or feet, adjusting the start height so toes stay clear, then moving on to placing leaf cards along the branch tips using frame sampling.

For the leaves, I'm figuring out the right orientation so they hang downward like eucalyptus foliage—working through the facing, lean, and flow parameters to get the card plane oriented correctly so leaves droop naturally from their branch attachment points.

I should bind static elements explicitly to the "stand" bone so they attach correctly to the root joint, and I'll need to import the frame helper. Now I'm thinking about the leaf texture setup, considering a small pixel-art size and color palette.

For the leaf drawing, I'm planning a lanceolate shape with a midrib, tapering to a point. Since the card hangs with a 180-degree lean, the stem needs to sit at the bottom row of the drawing so the leaf tip points downward once attached, widening around a third of the way up from the stem.

I'm shading the leaf with lighter left, darker right, and a pale midrib line, and planning a couple of palette variants for green-blue and olive tones. For gum nuts I'm clustering small brown spheres onto branches while keeping part counts low, and for the trunk I'm painting vertical bark streaks using cell coordinates.

I'm working out how to index streaks consistently by using angle around the trunk axis at the cell center instead of interpolated texel positions, since the latter causes inconsistent noise per texel — switching to atan2 on the cell's world position to compute a stable streak index.

Writing bark color logic...

I'll simplify the trunk to go straight down with minimal wobble, then add small knob spheres and peeling bark flap cards scattered along it for texture, positioning hands around where the trunk radius is about 0.052.

Now I'm working out the seat branch geometry extending from the trunk at y=0.36, tapering the radius so its top aligns with the koala's bottom around y=0.41, checking the clearances carefully.

I'm checking that the seat branch avoids colliding with the feet and legs, leaving a slight gap below the thighs, and deciding to skip a tail since koalas don't have one. I'm also planning to add a leaf and gumnut stub at the branch's far end, and now I'm listing out the skeleton joint hierarchy: stand, hips, spine1, spine2, neck, head.

Continuing the joint count, I'm adding jaw, ears, arm and leg chains, and finger/toe digit chains, bringing the total to roughly 60 joints, with eyes attaching to the head bone and digit names using side letters like L and R for uniqueness. I'm sketching out the sweep parameters for the hand digits with a small paw-colored radius and rounded caps.

Now I'm adding sharp claw spikes at each digit tip, oriented along the digit's chain direction using the chain's endpoint frame, then starting a reusable digit helper function...

Writing digit helper function...

I'm importing the Joint type for helper params and checking that unused imports don't trigger errors, then working out the wrist joint reference from the arm chain's final joint. Now I'm defining a function to compute wrap points for digit paths around a radius, mapping angles to 3D coordinates for the finger curvature.

For the hand placement I'm reasoning through which direction fingers versus thumbs should wrap—fingers curling toward the back of the trunk (+z, away from the koala's face) and thumbs wrapping forward, since the arm approaches the hand from the front-outer side of the body.

I'm also working out the dimensions for the palm pad and digit layout—wrist position, palm box sizing, and finger/thumb spacing based on the digit radius so they sit close enough to touch without overlapping.

Now setting up the foot toes with offset positions and a smaller sole pad, then the leg sweep using a radius chain that tapers from thigh to foot tip. After that I'm adding fur card scatters across the body surface for texture, filtering out hits that are too close together.

Designing a pixel-art tuft texture for the fur cards using a small grayscale palette.

Defining nostril and eye textures...

Still designing the ear texture grid...

For the geometry I'm checking that the circle shape will crop the texture corners to transparent naturally, and considering using a low-poly sphere for the ears with flat shading and a grayish fur tone. For facial details, I'm positioning the muzzle slightly lighter and forward on the head ellipsoid.

Working through the muzzle, nose, and trunk placement, I'm checking that their z-depths don't overlap—the nose front edge needs to stay just behind where the trunk's fork branches begin, so I'm nudging the muzzle and nose back slightly to keep clearance.

Now I'm positioning the lower jaw underneath the muzzle, figuring out a joint pivot point and a small cream-colored sphere to represent it, and planning a thin dark box to mark the mouth line.

Defining coat color palettes...

Still writing fur shading logic...

Now I'm moving on to the wooden plinth base, planning a pixel texture with plank rows sized so the top face tiles neatly across the 0.8x0.8 surface.

I'm layering a darker lower slab with a lighter upper slab trimmed slightly smaller, setting the trunk to start at y=0.09 once both plinth layers stack up. Then I'm adding decorative details on top -- moss patches, grass tufts, and fallen leaves as small flat cards scattered across the surface.

Now I'm adding a brass plaque to the front face and designing a tiny pixel font to spell out "KOALA" using 3x5 glyph grids for each letter.

I'll place the plaque texture on a thin box mounted to the front face of the lower slab, then scatter flat leaf cards across the plinth top for moss/litter detail, using random orientation and mirroring for a natural scattered look.

I also want a few gumnut/acorn spheres resting on the ground as separate merged parts, plus small hex-head brass screw cylinders at the corners of the upper slab, merged together with BufferGeometryUtils so their attributes stay consistent.

Actually, given the type-safety risk of importing from "three/addons," I'll skip merging altogether and just keep individual parts -- the total count is manageable, roughly 120 pieces once I tally the stand, trunk, body, and hand digits with their claws and palms. I'll scatter small gumnut spheres at branch fork points using positions sampled along the branch paths.

Still working out joint hierarchy...

I'm checking whether chains accept a role option for spine, neck, arms, and legs, and considering how the limb IK function handles roots, targets, lengths, and bend directions, especially for multi-segment versus single-segment cases.

Since I can't re-verify the ik.ts source now, I'll go with the documented interface: a list of arrays for bend directions, and pass point arrays directly as chain paths so the sweep smooths corners at joints like elbows.

For the body I'll use a bone list including spine and neck for the loft, apply coat color as the paint for sweeps, and keep texture resolution at the default 1024 since the total painted surface area (body, limbs, trunk, head) comfortably fits that texel density.

Settling on a 0.014 cell size for the 0.65m koala, giving the head about 20 cells wide. For the eyes, I'm placing small white boxes on the head bone, oriented outward using a direction vector so the local z-axis aims away from the face, mirrored for left/right with the sign factor.

Checking the eye position against the head's ellipsoid surface to make sure it's properly embedded—computing the implicit ellipsoid equation at the eye's x/y to solve for the matching z depth, confirming the eye sits roughly flush with a slight protrusion since the polygonal sphere mesh sits slightly inside the true ellipsoid surface. I'm also planning to add a darker patch around the eye for more expressiveness.

Designing a 7x7 pixel pattern for the eye texture with surrounding dark patch cells, a black pupil, and a white highlight for a lively stare.

Moving on to ear geometry now, positioning the scale, direction and joint hinge for the ears so they sit naturally against the head sphere.

Scattering tufts along the ear rim, filtering hits by normal direction to avoid the inner face, then doing a similar scatter across the head surface excluding the muzzle/eye region for fur cards.

For the body I'm sweeping fur cards across the sides and back, keeping density manageable since each card adds just a few triangles. Now I'm setting up bark flap cards along the trunk, scattering and filtering by height to avoid overlapping the hand regions, with bend and lean parameters to give the peeling bark some texture.

Writing bark texture pixels...

Now I'm defining the branch geometry for the tree's foliage, laying out point sequences and radii for each fork and side branch to build the skeletal structure.

Adding a small tail twig branch off the seat, checking its position relative to the koala's back so it stays plausible as the koala sits gripping the trunk while perched on the seat branch.

Now I'm scattering eucalyptus leaves along each branch, skipping the base and clustering more near the tips, with each leaf frame positioned along the sampled path and given a slight random lean so they hang naturally. I'm sizing the hanging leaves around 0.14 in length to feel proportionate to real eucalyptus foliage.

I define a deterministic flow function per leaf index to give horizontal drift direction, making sure to prefix the unused frame parameter to satisfy lint rules. With a 150° lean from the up axis blended with that flow direction, the leaves tilt downward and outward convincingly, and I'm adding some yaw variation for a more natural spread.

For leaf textures I'm picking two coloured variants, blue-green and olive-yellow, using plain white tint since the colors are baked into the texture. Since the leaf card normals face up like the frame axis, they'll catch light brightly.

Writing pixel texture code...

Now I'm thinking about resolution mismatch -- leaf textures at 9x24 are finer than the body's texel density, so I might switch to a chunkier 7x16 grid to keep things visually consistent.

For bark, I'm deciding branches and trunk share the same streaked paint logic for simplicity, with thinner younger branches possibly using a smoother greenish-gray tone instead of the rougher trunk texture.

Writing bark color palette...

Still writing bark shading logic...

I'm adding a transition ring color band for the eucalyptus-style pink-orange patch, then checking that color snapping keeps the total flat color count low, since only a few elements like claws and nose need distinct flat colors.

Now I'm planning the plinth top details: green moss boxes and small grass tufts rendered as pixel textures, plus a wood-colored tile texture for the base slab top and sides, and a few flat pixel leaves scattered as litter.

For the trunk base, I'm shaping a root flare using a lathe profile that widens slightly near the ground before tapering into the trunk, colored with bark paint and positioned to blend into the stand. I'm also double-checking the koala's seating position works fine on the branch before moving to other details.

Now I'm working out dark palm pads for the hands and underside, plus thinking about whether to add a small chin tuft. I'm verifying the head sphere properly contains the neck's loft geometry at the top, checking the shoulder bulge spheres protrude enough beyond the body's half-width to look like proper big arms, and setting up the arm bone chain from shoulder joint to hand target position.

I'm computing the elbow bend geometry using triangle law of cosines for the arm segment lengths, settling on 0.18 and 0.15 unit segments with a slight outward bend offset, then moving to set up similar distance and bend calculations for the hip-to-foot leg chain.

I'm now placing the smaller anatomical pieces: hip bulge spheres sized to meet the seat level, foot/palm box geometry positioned relative to the ankle and trunk radius so fingers start just outside the trunk surface, and setting the initial digit radius for the hand/foot segments.

Working out claw spikes with dark coloring, then setting up the finger and thumb chains sprouting from the wrist joint—spacing their y-offsets so fingers and thumbs sit on opposite sides without overlapping, and checking that left/right hand digits don't collide.

I'm adjusting the wrap angles to 0°, 35°, 70° so the digit endpoints spread far enough apart at the trunk's radius to avoid overlap, confirming thumbs stay clear of the chest, and mirroring the same digit-wrap logic for the feet at a lower trunk height, including big toes.

Setting up imports and starting to write the TypeScript file...

Defining color palettes...

Still writing coat shading logic...

Writing plank texture code...

Still defining plank fill logic...

Checking the plaque dimensions: 23 wide by 9 tall gives letters at rows 2-6 with proper top/bottom margins, and x-positions spaced by 4 for each letter leave a 2px margin on both sides.

Now I'm writing a leaf texture generator that varies width along the row using a sine curve, picking colors for the rib, highlight, midtone, and shadow based on position relative to center.

Checking the amplitude math keeps x1 within the grid bounds, then moving on to picking distinct color palettes for the two variants—highlight, mid, low, and rib tones for each.

Now I'm sketching a grass pixel texture, making sure every row string is exactly 7 characters wide using "g" and "h" markers mapped to a green base and lighter highlight color.

For the card texture, I'm laying out a small 5x8 "tuft" pattern with white and grey pixels to form a tufted shape.

Then I start writing the builder code for the koala model, creating a root "stand" joint and defining the spine as a joint chain built from a Catmull-Rom spline through four points, naming the segments hips, spine1, and spine2.

Next I add a short neck chain as a one-span polyline connecting the spine's top to the base of the skull, then attach a head joint at the end of that neck with a forward-tilted direction vector, confirming each parent-child relationship makes sense geometrically.

Finally I sketch out the body loft, sweeping station cross-sections along the spine and neck bones with the coat color, using 8-sided faceted (non-smooth) geometry to get a blocky, low-poly look, and start thinking through how the station widths and heights should be defined.

Now I'm working on the head shape itself — a scaled sphere part for the skull, then smaller spheres for the muzzle and jaw with their own paint ramps for lighter gray fur, plus planning the nose, eyes, cheek fluff cards, and a darker mouth-interior box, while checking that the jaw sphere sits properly below the head without visually clipping through it.

Writing ear loop...

Checking that the per-axis scale aligns correctly with the local orientation—z faces the direction vector, and the x/y scale values map to width and height as intended. Moving on to defining the inner ear part next.

Adding the inner ear circle part, verifying the direction and axis inputs line up with the facing convention so the circle renders flush against the front of the ear ellipsoid at the right offset distance.

Checking the gap at the rim with a smaller circle radius .04 gives a tolerable .007 gap, so I'll settle on radius .042 for the disc so it reads as a pad rather than poking through the ear.

For ear tufts, I'm scattering small tuft cards along the ear rim using surface points filtered by normal angle, then placing cards with a lean and cream color, confirming the hit normals and axis vectors line up and that bone weights carry correctly from the ear joint. Now moving on to building the arms, starting with the shoulder position for each side.

For the arm chain, I'm defining shoulder-to-hand limb points and building a chain joint structure (shoulder, elbow, wrist) parented to the chest spine joint, checking that the shoulder position falls within the correct spine bone segment and that the chain naming stays unique. I'm now working out the sweep radius profile for the arm mesh, tapering the thickness from shoulder to wrist with a hexagonal cross-section.

Adding a flat-shaded shoulder bulge sphere at the joint, then confirming the wrist is the last joint in the chain per the chain docs. Now I'm writing a `grip` helper to build the palm and fingers off the wrist joint, defining a point-wrapping function for placing digits around the hand and a `digit` helper that builds each finger as its own small chain with a tapered sweep.

Still writing digit helper...

Now working out the claw spike placed at the chain's end point, and figuring out how finger angles and the hand's radius should vary based on the trunk's taper function so the digits wrap naturally around the limb at different heights.

Checking that palm placement...

Now setting up the leg structure analogously, defining hip and foot positions and building limb points for the leg chain.

Checking clearance between the elbow and knee positions looks fine, and the leg sweep radii taper from .07 down to .036. I should also add a haunch feature.

Adding a hip sphere for contact, verifying the seat height clears the thigh bottom, and spacing the toe digits with the big toe wrapping the front. Now I'm moving to the trunk, building a tapered sweep path from the base up through the torso using collinear points along the vertical axis.

For the trunk itself, I'm considering adding bark knots and small branch stub spikes jutting outward near the back at a couple of heights to break up the straight cylinder and suggest where old branches once grew.

Now I'm looping through the branch specs, sweeping each one along a catmull curve with flat start caps fixed into the trunk and rounded tips, applying bark color and bone-stand smoothing — then placing leaf frames along each branch with extra clustered leaves near the tips.

Working out leaf jitter and yaw placement along the path, pooling all leaf frames into a single mesh call per texture since frames need no bones. I'm also planning gumnut clusters positioned at specific points along each branch's end.

Now I'm thinking through the stand's base structure, building a tiled plank box bone with randomized step offsets for the base slab, then a smaller upper slab sitting at a different height. I'm considering whether to reuse the same plank texture or generate a second lighter-toned variant so the two slabs read as visually distinct layers.

I'm adding brass corner cylinders at the upper slab's corners, sizing a front plaque to fit within the lower slab's height while keeping the koala-facing orientation correct, and planning scattered grass tuft decorations across the plinth's top surface.

Now I'm scattering grass tufts avoiding the trunk area, adding flat leaf litter cards with random yaw and mirrored texture variants, and placing a few small grey rotated stone boxes near the plinth base.

Skipping butterfly and mushroom extras for simplicity. For the koala, belly fur, claws, chin tuft, and cheek fur are already covered, so I'm now scattering body fur cards across the torso surface with filtered hit points, sized and leaned to follow the coat color.

I'm adding chest fluff with a smaller cream-colored card scatter, head cards filtered by cheeks and top of skull, and double-checking the nose box geometry with its white texture and slight forward tilt rotation.

Checking that trunk hits map to the stand weight correctly, and verifying the sweep function's overload signature works with a readonly radius array and color options.

Checking the remaining type signatures and unused-variable concerns to make sure everything compiles cleanly.

Now I'm double-checking that the various helper imports (noise, bayer, pick, pixelArt, snapColor, tileBox, cellPaint, pixelTexture) are all actually used, and verifying the Cell callback parameter types line up with the kit's definitions. I'm also starting to look for potential runtime issues, like whether `limb` correctly handles its bends parameter when passed either a single vector or an array.

I'm checking that the chain, lathe, and sweep calls match their expected signatures — outline points starting at x≥0 for the lathe, the segment count, and the 2-point sweep path defaulting roll correctly. I'm now tracing through the loft path with its catmull stations and bone spans for the spine and neck chains, making sure the neck span's projection onto the loft path is consistent and that the body sweep's loft length properly accounts for where the neck chain begins.

I'm verifying the frame and flow function signatures for cards, checking type compatibility for direction arrays and scatter filter callbacks, and confirming surface acceptance for Part types. Then I'm working out leaf and tuft card sizing against grid resolution to keep texel aspect ratios square — settling on roughly [0.05, 0.13] for leaves and a matching square ratio for the tuft cards' 5x8 grid.

I'm sizing the grass and bark flap cards similarly, confirming part counts are fine, and setting up a seeded rng for grass placement. I'm making sure every shape always gets an explicit color rather than relying on nearest-part inheritance, keeping the flat color palette under 64 entries by using white for textured parts and distinct hex values for claws, nuts, stones, brass, and mouth. I'm also placing gum nuts along the path with jittered offsets and double-checking the Joint type import path.

Now I'm writing the trunk radius function and a grip helper that generates finger/thumb joints around the trunk circumference using angle and radius calculations, distinguishing hands from feet with different name prefixes like finger/toe and thumb/bigToe.

Checking the tangent direction at a=1.22 — it points inward toward the back center line, so the claw curls inward digging toward the trunk rather than outward; a length of .02 should work.

Now I'm confirming the arm and hand positions relative to the trunk, making sure the palms sit within x=.06 and the arms pass in front toward the trunk side correctly, before assembling the stand parts and writing the final code with the meta description.

Confirming other indexed accesses like `boneJoints![i]` and `GLYPH[ch]` are fine given noUnchecked is off, and the arm/spine joint indexing checks out too. Now I'm ready to assemble the final file text, double-checking the bone arrays for sweeps like the hip-to-spine-to-neck chain.

Now I'm writing the plank texture generator, drawing horizontal wood rows with randomized shading and staggered board-end seams, plus a pass to add nail dots near each seam using a slightly different tan color.
